title: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha
summary: Siddhartha Gautama, a teacher born into the Shakya clan on the India–Nepal border plain, founded the movement now called Buddhism. Scholars place his life in the sixth to fourth centuries BCE and still disagree by roughly eighty years.
card: Tradition says he was born at Lumbini, left his family home at twenty-nine, awakened at Bodh Gaya at thirty-five, preached first at Sarnath and died at Kushinagar aged eighty after forty-five years of teaching. The older scholarly dating, about 563–483 BCE, has been challenged by arguments for a death near 404 BCE, so no single year is settled. Archaeology confirms the sacred sites and Ashoka's later pilgrimage but not the details of the biography.
what:
Siddhartha Gautama (Pali Siddhattha Gotama), later called the Buddha, 'the awakened one', and Shakyamuni, 'sage of the Shakya clan', is the founder of Buddhism. Our knowledge of him comes from texts first set down in writing long after his death, and from monuments built by later believers, so a historian can say with reasonable confidence that he lived and taught in the middle Ganges region, but must treat most of the biography as tradition.

That tradition says he was born in the garden of Lumbini to the ruling family of the Shakya clan, in the area of the present India–Nepal border. Stories of a miraculous conception and birth were added later and are recorded here as belief. He grew up in comfort, at about twenty-nine left his home, wife and young son, and spent six years among wandering ascetics. When extreme fasting failed him, he sat beneath a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya and, at about thirty-five, attained bodhi, the awakening that tradition says ends suffering. He gave his first sermon in a deer park at Sarnath near Benares, taught for the remaining forty-five years of his life across north-eastern India, and died at Kushinagar aged eighty. His cremated remains were divided among followers and enshrined in burial mounds.

The dates are disputed. Theravada tradition gives 623–543 BCE; the long chronology, based on a gap of about 218 years between his death and Ashoka's consecration, gives roughly 566–486 BCE or 563–483 BCE. Texts preserved in East Asia imply only about a hundred years between the two, and many specialists now favour a later death, around 405 BCE; Richard Gombrich argues for about 404 BCE. Which Kapilavastu he grew up in is also disputed between Tilaurakot in Nepal and Piprahwa in India. In 2013 excavators reported a timber structure of the sixth century BCE under the Maya Devi Temple at Lumbini, but whether it honoured the Buddha's birth is an interpretation.

uncertainty.note: Pin uses the long chronology (birth c. 563 BCE = year -562; death c. 483 BCE = year -482). The Theravada traditional dates (623–543 BCE; UNESCO states birth in 623 BC) lie about 60 years earlier; the short-chronology proposals (Gombrich c. 484–404 BCE, SEP 'around 405 BCE' for death; Choong lists 466–386 and 448–368 BCE) lie up to about 80 years later. No date within these bounds is established.

how: No contemporary document survives, so the sequence below combines tradition with what archaeology can confirm. Tradition says he was born at Lumbini and raised in luxury at Kapilavastu. At about twenty-nine he left home after meeting an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic, joined teachers of the shramana (wandering renouncer) movement, found them unsatisfactory and practised severe fasting for six years. Abandoning extremes, he meditated at Bodh Gaya and attained awakening at about thirty-five. After several weeks nearby, he taught at Sarnath, then spent forty-five years walking and teaching in north-eastern India, gathering monks, nuns and lay followers. He died at Kushinagar at eighty, reportedly after a meal of tainted food, and his body was cremated. Relics were divided among groups of followers and placed in hemispherical mounds, some of which became pilgrimage sites. The archaeological anchors are Ashoka's inscribed pillar at Lumbini and his first temple at Bodh Gaya, both third century BCE, plus a 2013 report of a sixth-century BCE timber structure at Lumbini.
why_it_matters: Siddhartha Gautama's teaching became the basis of Buddhism, a tradition that, according to a 2013 National Geographic Society release, counts roughly half a billion adherents. Within a few centuries of his death the emperor Ashoka visited Lumbini, set up an inscribed pillar and built the first temple at Bodh Gaya, so the birthplace and the place of awakening became fixed pilgrimage destinations that still draw hundreds of thousands of visitors each year and are listed as UNESCO World Heritage properties. The four sites tied to his life (birth, awakening, first sermon and death) organised later Buddhist art, with the Eight Great Events codified in India by about 700–1200 CE. Because his dates are uncertain by about eighty years, he is also a test case for how far Indian history can be anchored: the long and short chronologies shift the whole sequence of early Indian religious and political history, including how his lifetime relates to the Maurya emperor Ashoka. Had he not founded a community that preserved and transmitted his teaching, there would be no Buddhist monastic order to carry it across Asia, and the Buddha-titled sites at Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar would have no common story to unite them. Debate about Kapilavastu and Lumbini's earliest shrine continues to shape Nepali and Indian heritage claims today.

beats.caption: He leaves home and practises asceticism for six years before turning to the middle way.
At Bodh Gaya, beneath a pipal tree, he attains the awakening that makes him the Buddha.
He delivers his first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath near Benares and begins gathering followers.
For forty-five years he walks and teaches across north-eastern India.
He dies at Kushinagar; his cremated remains are divided among followers and enshrined in burial mounds, the first Buddhist pilgrimage sites.
Roughly two centuries later Emperor Ashoka raises an inscribed pillar at Lumbini, fixing the birthplace as a pilgrimage destination that still draws pilgrims.

perspectives.holder: Long chronology (Theravada tradition and many 20th-century scholars)
perspectives.account: The Buddha died about 218 years before Ashoka's consecration; with Ashoka placed c. 268 BCE from edicts naming Hellenistic kings, he lived c. 566–486 BCE, and the Met cites 563–483 BCE. The Theravada tradition itself reckons 623–543 BCE, which UNESCO repeats for his birth.

perspectives.holder: Short chronology (East Asian Sanskrit-tradition sources; Gombrich; SEP)
perspectives.account: Sanskrit sources preserved in East Asia put only about a hundred years between his death and Ashoka. Gombrich argues from a lineage of Vinaya masters in the Dipavamsa for a death c. 404 BCE (422–399 BCE); the SEP notes many scholars now date the death around 405 BCE, and Choong lists proposals of 466–386 and 448–368 BCE.

perspectives.holder: Tilaurakot case (Coningham and Nepali colleagues; P. C. Mukherji 1890s)
perspectives.account: Tilaurakot in Nepal is the Shakya capital Kapilavastu; excavations found occupation between the seventh and fifth centuries BCE, and Coningham sees little reason to doubt the nineteenth-century identification.

After a 1962 excavation judged that Tilaurakot's earliest settlement postdates the Buddha, Indian archaeologists identified Piprahwa, in Uttar Pradesh, as Kapilavastu, citing its earliest remains of a third-century BCE monastery.

perspectives.holder: Coningham et al. (2013) on Lumbini's earliest shrine
perspectives.account: The team reports a sixth-century BCE timber structure around an open central space beneath the Maya Devi Temple and links it to a tree shrine and the nativity story; the release itself calls that link a postulate, so the structure shows early ritual activity at the site but does not by itself fix the Buddha's date.
